Status of Claims

Applicant submits this Amendment and Response to address the non-final Office Action dated May 4, 2023. Claims 1 and 5 are amended, claims 18-20 are cancelled, and claims 2 1-23 are added, without adding any new matter and without intending to abandon or dedicate to the public any patentable subject matter. Claims 9-17 remain withdrawn. Therefore, 1-8 and 21-23 are present for examination. Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration of this application as amended.
Interpretation of Claim Elements under 35 U.S.C. §112(f)
Claims 1, 4, 5, and 7 have been considered to invoke 35 U.S.C. §112(f). More

specifically, the Office Action states that the terms "first tracking device," "second tracking device," and "optical imaging device" recited in claims 1, 4, 5, and 7 are being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. @ 112(f) because they use a generic placeholder that is coupled with functional language without reciting sufficient structure to perform the recited function. See Office A ction p.
According to MPEP @2181(I), a claim limitation should be interpreted according to 112(f) if it meets the following 3-Prong analysis:
(1) the claim limitation uses the phrase "means" or a term used as a substitute for "means" that is a generic placeholder;
(2) the phrase "means", or the substitute term is modified by functional language, typically linked by the transition word "for" or another linking word; and
(3) the phrase "means" or the substitute term is not modified by sufficient structure or material for performing the claimed function.
In addition, MPEP @2181(I) provides that:
By contrast, a claim limitation that does not use the term "means" or
"step" will trigger the rebuttable presumption that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph does not apply. See, e.g., Phillips v. A WH Corp., 415
Fitness, Inc. v. Brunswick Corp., 288 F.3d 1359, 1369, 62 USPQ2d 1658, 1664

(Fed. Cir. 2002); Personalized Media Commc'ns, LL Cv. ITC, 161 F.3d 696, 703- 04, 48 USPQ2d 1880, 1886-87 (Fed. Cir. 1998). This presumption is a strong one that is not readily overcome. Lighting World, Inc. v. Birchwood Lighting,
Thyssenkrupp Elevator Americas Corp., 649 F.3d 1350, 1356, 99 USPQ2d 1112,
1117 (Fed. Cir. 2011). This strong presumption may be overcome if the claim
limitation is shown to use a non-structural term that is "a nonce word or a verbal
construct that is not recognized as the name of structure" but is merely a substitute
for the term "means" associated with functional language. Lighting World, 382
F.3d at 1360, 72 USPQ2d at 1350. The substitute term in such cases acts as a
generic placeholder for the term "means" and would not be recognized by one of
ordinary skill in the art as being sufficiently definite structure for performing
the claimed function.
See, e.g., MPEP § 2181(I) (emphases added).

Applicant submits that the phrases "first tracking device," "second tracking device," and "optical imaging device" should not be considered to invoke 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) because the 3- Prong analysis for each is not met.

Applicant submits that the phrases "first tracking device" and "second tracking device" provides sufficient structure to perform the recited function, and that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the phrases "first tracking device" and "second tracking device" as providing sufficient structure for performing the claimed function. Rather than operating as a generic placeholder for the term "means" or "step," the phrases "first tracking device" and "second tracking device" are a definite structural term for performing the claimed function. Accordingly, the phrases "first tracking device" and "second tracking device" do not operate as a generic placeholder for the word "means" or "step," and should not considered to invoke 35 U.S.C. §112(f).

Applicant submits that the phrase "optical imaging device" is proceeded by a sufficient structural modifier, such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the phrase "optical imaging device" as having sufficient structure. Indeed, the word "optical" sufficiently modifies the word "imaging device," such that the term "optical imaging device" does not operate as a generic placeholder for the phrase "means." Accordingly, the phrase "optical imaging device" does not operate as a generic placeholder for the word "means" or "step," and should not considered to invoke 35 U.S.C. § 112(f).
In view of the foregoing, Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration of the interpretation of claims 1, 4, 5, and 7 under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f).
Claim 5 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) as failing to comply with the written
description requirement and more specifically, that the disclosure does not provide a detailed

explanation for how a probe is used to verify a pose of one or more anatomical elements. To further prosecution, the term "probe" has been amended to "navigation probe," which would be known to one skilled in the art as capable of verifying a pose of one or more anatomical elements. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests that the rejection of claim 5 under 35 U.S.C. § 112 be withdrawn.

Claims 1-8 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. §101 as the Office Action alleges that the claims do not amount to significantly more than an abstract idea. Applicant respectfully traverses this rejection and requests it be withdrawn for at least the following reasons.

The current test to determine whether a claim is directed toward patent eligible subject matter is the analysis based upon Alice Corp. Pty. Ltd. v. CLS Bank Int'l., 134 S. Ct. 2347 (2014) (hereinafter "Alice") and Mayo Collaborative Services v. Prometheus Laboratories, Inc., 132 S. Ct. 1289 (2011) (hereinafter "Mayo"). This test is essentially in two parts. "Supreme Court precedent instructs us to 'first determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept."' Enfish, LLC v. Microsoft Corp., No. 2015-2044, slip op. at *9 (Fed. Cir. May 12, 2016) (quoting Alice, at 2347) (hereinafter "Enfish").
As "[t]he Supreme Court has not established a definitive rule to determine what

constitutes as an 'abstract idea' sufficient to satisfy the first step of the Mayo/Alice inquiry," the Court has "found it sufficient to compare claims at issue to those claims already found to be directed to an abstract idea in previous cases." Id. (citing Alice). "If this threshold determination is met, we move to the second step of the inquiry and 'consider the elements of each claim both individually and "as an ordered combination" to determine whether the additional elements "transform the nature of the claim" into a patent-eligible application."' Id. (quoting Alice (quoting Mayo)).
The analysis of the claims at issue will be presented below, discussing the claims in Parts 1, 2A and 2B.
Step 1 - Determine whether the claim is directed to one of the statutory categories of invention.
Step 2A - If the claim is directed to one of the statutory categories of invention, determine if the claim is, as a whole, directed to a judicial exception.

Step 2B - If the claim is, as a whole, directed to a judicial exception, analyze the claim elements, both individually and as a whole, to determine if there are additional limitations that amount to significantly more than the abstract idea.

As explained below, the claims satisfy Part 1 as they are directed to at least one of the statutory categories of invention, as well as Part 2A, as the claims are not directed to a judicially recognized exception. While analysis under Part 2B should not be required, the claims also satisfy the significantly more than an abstract idea test for a number of reasons, including the fact that the claims are specifically limited to a specific technical field. For these reasons, as discussed below, the claims are directed to patent-eligible subject matter.
Step 1: The claims are directed to one of the statutory categories of invention.
Applicant agrees with the Examiner that all of the claims meet the requirements of step
Step 2A: Prong One - Evaluate Whether the Claim Recites a Judicial Exception
The Office Action asserts that the claims recite an abstract idea that falls into the
"Mental Processes" groupings. See Office Action pp. 6-7. Applicant respectfully disagrees.

Initially, Applicant submits that the claims are not directed toward mental processes. The October 2019 Update to the Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility ("October 2019 Update") states that "[c]laims do not recite a mental process when they do not contain limitations that can practically be performed in the human mind." See October 2019 Update p. 2 (Notice provided at 84 Fed. Reg. 55942 (Oct. 18, 2019); substance of the Update published at https://www.uspto.gov) (emphasis added). Claim 1 recites, inter alia, receiving a first dataset containing a first image depicting the first tracking device and the second tracking device, receiving a second dataset containing a second image depicting the first tracking device and the second tracking device, processing each of the first image and the second image using an image processing algorithm to identify the first tracking device and the second tracking device, and determining a first relative pose of the first tracking device relative to the second tracking device from the processed first image and a second relative pose of the first tracking device relative to the second tracking device from the processed second image. Applicant respectfully submits that such actions cannot be practically performed in the human mind. For

example, the first image and the second image are processed using an image processing algorithm, an action that cannot be practically performed in the human mind. Accordingly, the claims are not directed toward mental processes.
Since the pending claims are not directed toward an abstract idea, the pending claims are patent eligible. Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejection.
Step 2A: Prong Two - Evaluate Whether the Claim, As a Whole, Integrates the Recited Judicial Exception into a Practical Application of the Exception
Although Applicant believes the claims are not directed toward a judicial exception,

and that further analysis under Step 2A, Prong Two is believed to be redundant, the claims are directed toward a practical application for at least the reason that they integrate the alleged judicial exception into a practical application.

The October 2019 Update indicates that "[in order to determine whether the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or other technology], first the specification should be evaluated to determine if the disclosure provides sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The specification need not explicitly set forth the improvement, but it must describe the invention such that the improvement would be apparent to one of ordinary skill in the art." Id. at 12. Then, "the claim must be evaluated to ensure that the claim itself reflect the disclosed improvement." Id. at 12.

As discussed in the application as-filed, patient movement during a surgical operation in which navigation is used can present issues. Registration of the patient to a navigation system or a navigated item may include scanning the patient and the navigated item to determine a spatial correlation between the patient and the navigated item. See Application as- published [0046]. However, if the patient moves during the surgical operation, the registration may be invalid or inaccurate. Id. The application as-filed then provides a solution by providing a tracking marker on a table on which the patient is positioned on and a tracking marker on the patient (or an anatomical element of the patient). The tracking markers are captured in image or sensor data from which the relative poses of the tracking markers can be
determined. Id., at [0048]. The relative poses can then be compared to determine if the patient has moved relative to the table during the surgical operation. Id.

The use of these technical solutions help ensure proper registration during the surgical operation. Applicant submits that a person of ordinary skill in the art would, when viewing such a detailed disclosure, recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement.
Moreover, such technical solutions are recited by the claims. Indeed, independent claim

1 recites a first tracking device affixed to a table and a second tracking device affixed to an anatomical element, the anatomical element having a pose relative to the table, receiving a first dataset, the first dataset containing a first image depicting the first tracking device and the second tracking device, receiving a second dataset, the second dataset containing second image depicting the first tracking device and the second tracking device, processing each of the first image and the second image using an image processing algorithm to identify the first tracking device and the second tracking device, determining a first relative pose of the first tracking device relative to the second tracking device from the processed first image and a second relative pose of the first tracking device relative to the second tracking device from the processed second image, and comparing the first relative pose and the second relative pose to determine if a relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed. Applicant submits that these claim features recite the disclosed improvement to ensuring an accurate registration. Accordingly, the claim as a whole integrates the alleged judicial exception into a practical application.
Step 2B

Although Applicant submits that the currently pending claims are patent eligible under a Step 2A analysis as discussed above, Applicant also submits that the claims recite additional hardware elements that are sufficient to amount to "significantly more" than an abstract idea. For example, by affixing a first tracking device to a table and a second tracking device to an anatomical element having a pose relative to the table, patient movement relative to the table can be monitored. Thus, the claims amount to "significantly more" than an abstract idea.

For at least the foregoing reasons, Applicant respectfully submits that the second prong of the eligibility test properly results in a determination of patent-eligibility, and respectfully requests that the rejection of claims 1-8 under 35 U.S.C. § 101 be withdrawn.

Claims 1, 2, 7, and 8 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by International Patent Publication No. 2020/072335 to Nikou et al. ("Nikou"). Claims 3-5 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being obvious over Nikou and further in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 2014/0206990 to Epstein et al. ("Epstein"). Claim 6 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being obvious over Nikou and further in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 2019/0090955 to Singh et al. ("Singh").

Anticipation under 35 U.S.C. § 102 requires that the reference teach every aspect of the claimed invention either explicitly or impliedly. See MPEP §706.02. "[U]nless a reference discloses within the four corners of the document not only all of the limitations claimed but also all of the limitations arranged or combined in the same way as recited in the claim, it cannot be said to prove prior invention of the thing claimed, and, thus, cannot anticipate under 35 U.S.C. §102." Net Moneyin, Inc. v. Verisign, Inc., 545 F.3d 1359, 1371 (Fed. Cir. 2008); 88 U.S.P.Q.2d

To establish aprimafacie case of obviousness, all claim limitations must first be taught or suggested by the prior art. See, e.g., DyStar Textilfarben GmbH & Co. Deutschland KG v. C.H. Patrick Co., 464 F.3d 1356, 1360 (Fed. Cir. 2006); 80 U.S.P.Q.2d 1641, 1645 (2006). "All

words in a claim must be considered in judging the patentability of that claim against the prior art." MPEP § 2143.03 (citing In re Wilson, 424 F.2d 1382, 1385, 165 USPQ 494, 496 (CCPA 1970)). The Examiner must then provide an explicit analysis of the motivation for combining the references. See KSR Int'l Co. v. Teleflex Inc., 550 U.S. 398, 418 (2007); 82 U.S.P.Q.2d 1385, 1396 (2007) ("a patent composed of several elements is not proved obvious merely by demonstrating that each of its elements was, independently, known in the prior art . . .."). While the Examiner can choose one of several exemplary rationales from the MPEP to support an obviousness rejection, all the rationales in the MPEP still require the Examiner to demonstrate that all the claim elements are shown in the prior art. See MPEP § 2143, Original Ninth Edition, March 2014.

Claim 1 recited, inter alia, receiving a first dataset, the first dataset containing a first image depicting the first tracking device and the second tracking device, receiving a second dataset, the second dataset containing a second image depicting the first tracking device and the

second tracking device, processing each of the first image and the second image using an image processing algorithm to identify the first tracking device and the second tracking device, determining a first relative pose of the first tracking device relative to the second tracking device from the processed first image and a second relative pose of the first tracking device relative to the second tracking device from the processed second image, and comparing the first relative pose and the second relative pose to determine if a relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed. None of the cited references taken together or separately appear to disclose, teach, or suggest the features recited in the amended claims.
Nikou teaches a system for performing a computer-aided surgical procedure in which

optical sensors detect and record the location of one or more optical tracking devices mounted to a patient. Nikou, Abstract. Nikou, however, does not teach receiving a first dataset, the first dataset containing a first image depicting the first tracking device and the second tracking device, receiving a second dataset, the second dataset containing a second image depicting the first tracking device and the second tracking device, processing each of the first image and the second image using an image processing algorithm to identify the first tracking device and the second tracking device, determining a first relative pose of the first tracking device relative to the second tracking device from the processed first image and a second relative pose of the first tracking device relative to the second tracking device from the processed second image, and comparing the first relative pose and the second relative pose to determine if a relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed as recited in claim 1. Thus, Nikou does not disclose or teach the claimed limitations of claim 1.

Epstein does not cure the deficiencies of Nikou. Epstein teaches a method for verifying a spatial registration of an anatomical region by tracking a spatial pose of at least one checkpoint defined within the anatomical region and tracking a spatial pose of a probe tip in proximity to the anatomical region at the checkpoint. Epstein, Abstract. Epstein, however, does not teach receiving a first dataset, the first dataset containing a first image depicting the first tracking device and the second tracking device, receiving a second dataset, the second dataset containing a second image depicting the first tracking device and the second tracking device, processing each of the first image and the second image using an image processing algorithm to identify the first tracking device and the second tracking device, determining a first relative pose of the first tracking device relative to the second tracking device from the processed first image and a

second relative pose of the first tracking device relative to the second tracking device from the processed second image, and comparing the first relative pose and the second relative pose to determine if a relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed as recited in claim 1. Thus, Epstein does not disclose or teach the claimed limitations of claim 1.

Singh does not cure the deficiencies of Nikou. Singh teaches systems and methods for estimating a pose of an anatomy and a pose of a surgical instrument relative to the anatomy by receiving visual and sensory information indicative of pose of the anatomy and surgical instruments relative to the anatomy. Singh, Abstract. Singh, however, does not teach receiving a first dataset, the first dataset containing a first image depicting the first tracking device and the second tracking device, receiving a second dataset, the second dataset containing a second image depicting the first tracking device and the second tracking device, processing each of the first image and the second image using an image processing algorithm to identify the first tracking device and the second tracking device, determining a first relative pose of the first tracking device relative to the second tracking device from the processed first image and a second relative pose of the first tracking device relative to the second tracking device from the processed second image, and comparing the first relative pose and the second relative pose to determine if a relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed as recited in claim 1. Thus, Singh does not disclose or teach the claimed limitations of claim 1.

Accordingly, the combination of Nikou, Epstein, and/or Singh fails to disclose every limitation of claims 1-8, and for at least this reason, Applicant respectfully requests that the rejection of claims 1-8 under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 & 103 be withdrawn.
New claims 21-23

Independent claim 21 is newly added and recites, inter alia, receiving a first dataset, the first dataset containing first sensor data corresponding to the first tracking device and the second tracking device, receiving a second dataset, the second dataset containing second sensor data corresponding to the first tracking device and the second tracking device, processing each of the first sensor data and the second sensor data to identify the first tracking device and the second tracking device, determining a first relative pose of the first tracking device relative to the second tracking device from the processed first sensor data and a second relative pose of the first

tracking device relative to the second tracking device from the processed second sensor data, and comparing the first relative pose and the second relative pose to determine if a relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed." Support for claim 21 can be found in the as-filed Specification at, for example, at paragraph [0060].

As similarly discussed above, none of the cited prior art references teach or disclose receiving a first dataset, the first dataset containing first sensor data corresponding to the first tracking device and the second tracking device, receiving a second dataset, the second dataset containing second sensor data corresponding to the first tracking device and the second tracking device, processing each of the first sensor data and the second sensor data to identify the first tracking device and the second tracking device, determining a first relative pose of the first tracking device relative to the second tracking device from the processed first sensor data and a second relative pose of the first tracking device relative to the second tracking device from the processed second sensor data, and comparing the first relative pose and the second relative pose to determine if a relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has change. Thus, the references Nikou, Epstein, and/or Singh do not teach or disclose the claimed limitations of claim 21 and claims 22 and 23 which depend from claim 21. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests entry and allowance of claims 21-23.

Based upon the foregoing, Applicant believes that all pending claims are in condition for allowance and such disposition is respectfully requested. Applicant does not acquiesce to any objection, rejection, or argument not specifically addressed herein. Rather, Applicant believes the amendments and arguments contained herein overcome all objections, rejections, or arguments.
